## Introduction
  The main goal of this project is to replicate the results from Experiment 2 of the Lopez-Brau & Ettinger (2023) paper. A secondary goal of this project is to partially replicate the results from Experiment 3a of the same paper. The paper broadly revolves around the inferences humans make about the social meaning of objects, specifically investigating whether adults are able to infer the communicative meaning of objects from their placement. Experiment 2 finds that adults believe that objects that impose a low cost on deciders are more likely to be communicative relative to objects that do not impose a cost. Experiment 3 furthers these findings: adults infer that a low-cost object in front of a door serves as a signal communicated by the person who placed the object that others should avoid that door. I anticipate leading projects on similar questions to investigate what inferences children make about the social meaning of objects. Replicating the methods and analysis will therefore be beneficial, serving as background findings motivating my studies and as a first step to brainstorming potential project designs and analysis plans for my own studies.  
  
  There will be two parts of the replication project. The first part will include stimuli that consists of eight sets of images. Each set will have a pair of doors side-by-side: one “low-cost door” (object placed in front of the door) and one “no-cost door” (object placed beside the door). The objects will be a plant, a chair, a pile of books, a pile of cinderblocks, some tape, some meter sticks, a hat, and a fishbowl tied to a tack on a door frame. Participants will be asked to imagine leaving an office and encountering this pair of doors. They will be asked a series of multiple-choice questions: an attention-check (“What objects are in front of the doors?”), test trial (“Which door do you think someone was trying to tell you something?”), a manipulation check (“Which door requires more work to walk through?”) and lastly, an inclusion question (“Do you think you would be able to walk through this door if you wanted to?”). These methods will match the procedure from Experiment 2 of the paper.
  The second part will include stimuli that consists of 8 more images of pairs of doors, with each pair consisting
of an empty door and a door with an object placed directly in the middle of one of the doorways. Half of these door pairs will be open and the other half will be closed. The objects will be the same as listed above and participants will again be asked to imagine leaving an office and encountering this pair of doors. Participants will then answer: an attention-check (“What is the only difference between the two exits?”), test trial (“What do you think someone was trying to tell you about the door with the object?”; the options provided will be (a) “You should walk through the door with the object” and (b) “You should not walk through the door with the object”), manipulation-check (same as Exp 2), an inclusion questions (same as Exp 2). These methods are a shortened version of the procedure from Experiment 3a of the paper (only including the "low-cost" condition) to account for time constraints of running the replication on SONA.

  I anticipate the main challenges to be setting up the paradigm, specifically programming it using JavaScript which is unfamiliar to me. I imagine that it might be further challenging to code the study design such that failure on the attention checks reroutes participants to the start of the story and does not allow them to continue with the experiment until they pass the check (as per the published study design). I also anticipate collecting data from SONA to be challenging as the process is new to me.
  I hope to learn more about coding a jsPsych experiment and collecting data from an adult sample. Gaining skills in carrying out a jsPsych experiment and collecting data on SONA may both be helpful in the case I need to run or pilot studies on adult samples. Given some familiarity I have with running behavioral studies along with transparent materials and code provided by the authors, I am optimistic that this project will be feasible over the course of this quarter. More importantly, I hope to gain familiarity with how to replicate findings from a published project: from finding relevant materials and files from the original paper, to recreating the methods for data collection, all the way to rerunning the original analyses on my dataset and writing them up.
  
Link to my repository: https://github.com/anlaha/lopez-brau2023; Original Paper hosted on repository at: https://github.com/anlaha/lopez-brau2023/tree/main/original_paper
